To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the intracellular localization of ANT is consistent with a role in the regulation of ATP synthesis in the mitochondria of Drosophila flight muscles.

1) Drosophila flight muscles have high ANT levels, 2) the ANT in flight muscles is predominantly in the mitochondria, and 3) ANT is not in a mitochondrial subcompartment, the cristae, but rather in a non-cristae subcompartment.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the mitochondrial adenine nucleotide translocase (ANT), a key protein in the mitochondrial permeability transition (mPT) pore, is not required for the mPT in Drosophilain vitro orin vivo.
ANT, a protein that has been studied in the context of mammalian metabolism and mitochondrial function, has a role in the regulation of muscle function in the Drosophila indirect flight muscle.
ANT is not only localized in the mitochondria, but also in the sarcoplasm, where it may be involved in the regulation of intracellular calcium.
